name: Sofpironium bromide (Sofdra)

lead: Sofpironium bromide is a prescription underarm gel taken up by people who want dry underarms and no sweat marks on clothing.

It is an anticholinergic that blocks muscarinic M3 receptors on sweat glands at the application site, which reduces the signal that triggers sweating. It was approved in Japan in 2020 as Ecclock and in the US in 2024 as Sofdra. Phase 2 and 3 vehicle-controlled trials have evaluated it, a Japanese open-label study followed patients for 52 weeks, and a 2025 systematic review assessed it.

paras: It is applied as a gel to the underarms in people diagnosed with primary axillary hyperhidrosis. It is a sweat treatment rather than a general cosmetic product.

The US label lists dry mouth, blurred vision, application-site pain, redness and irritation, dilated pupils and urinary retention as the most common adverse reactions, and warns of lack of sweating in hot environments. It is prescription-only in the US and Japan.

angle.text: Sofpironium bromide is a prescription underarm gel approved in Japan (2020) and the US (2024) for heavy sweating, used by people who want dry underarms and no sweat marks on clothing. It blocks the signal that triggers sweat glands. Its trials were run in people diagnosed with hyperhidrosis.

lead: Sofpironium bromide is a prescription gel applied to the underarms to reduce sweating. It is a topical anticholinergic approved for primary axillary hyperhidrosis, meaning excessive underarm sweating without an underlying medical cause. By cutting the amount of sweat produced at the application site, it addresses the visible damp patches, stained shirts and yellowing fabric that people with the condition describe as their main appearance concern. [1][2]

The compound was developed by Bodor Laboratories, licensed to Brickell Biotech (development code BBI-4000), and approved in Japan in 2020 as Ecclock and in the United States in 2024 as Sofdra. [3][4][2] In Japan the product is marketed by Kaken Pharmaceutical, while the US approval was announced by Botanix Pharmaceuticals. [4]

Research on the drug consists of medical trials in people diagnosed with hyperhidrosis rather than cosmetic studies. Phase 2 and phase 3 randomized, vehicle-controlled trials have measured sweat weight, symptom scores and quality of life; a 52-week open-label study in Japan followed patients over the longer term; and several systematic reviews and meta-analyses have pooled the randomized results. [1][5][6][7][8][9]
infobox: Bodor Laboratories; licensed to Brickell Biotech

paras: Sofpironium bromide is a quaternary ammonium salt with the molecular formula C22H32BrNO5 and a molar mass of about 470 g/mol. [4] It was designed using a retrometabolic approach: the molecule is meant to act at the skin and then be broken down rapidly once it reaches the bloodstream, which developers say limits the systemic anticholinergic effects seen with older drugs in this class. [10][11]

Hyperhidrosis is defined as sweating beyond what body temperature regulation requires. The focal primary form usually begins in adolescence or earlier, affects men and women about equally, and often runs in families. [12] Surveys summarized on Wikipedia report that a large majority of affected people describe moderate to severe emotional impact, including frequent shirt changes and avoidance of certain clothing. [12]

For most patients the appearance payoff is the practical one: drier underarms, fewer visible sweat patches on shirts and less staining of fabric. In the trials, one co-primary outcome was the Hyperhidrosis Disease Severity Scale (HDSS), a patient-reported measure in which a score of 1 or 2 indicates sweating that is tolerable or never interferes with daily activities. [1][5] Quality of life was measured with the Dermatology Life Quality Index (DLQI), and the pooled analyses report larger DLQI improvements with the gel than with vehicle. [9][6]

The US label indicates Sofdra for primary axillary hyperhidrosis in adults and in children aged 9 and older. [2] In Japan the 5% gel was approved for the same condition. [3] Studies have also been registered in palmar hyperhidrosis and in pediatric patients. [13][14] A small Japanese crossover study separately examined the gel for clozapine-induced hypersalivation, a different use of the same anticholinergic action. [15]

Established options for axillary hyperhidrosis include prescription-strength aluminium chloride antiperspirants, topical glycopyrronium tosylate (approved by the FDA in 2018), botulinum toxin injections that last roughly three to nine months, oral anticholinergics, and devices such as microwave thermolysis. [12][16] Sofpironium is one of the newer topical entrants alongside glycopyrronium. [16][17]

Eccrine sweat glands are stimulated by acetylcholine acting on M3 muscarinic receptors. Sofpironium bromide competitively inhibits those receptors at the site of application, which reduces the signal that triggers sweating. [3][2]
The retrometabolic design is intended to make the molecule a so-called soft drug: effective where it is applied but rapidly metabolized to inactive products after absorption. [11]

According to the US label, the most common adverse reactions (2% or more) are dry mouth, blurred vision, application-site pain, erythema, dermatitis, pruritus and irritation, dilated pupils and urinary retention. [2]

The label's warnings cover use with caution in people with a history of urinary retention, watching for a general lack of sweating in hot environments, and avoiding driving or machinery if blurred vision occurs. [2] Meta-analyses of randomized trials report higher rates of anticholinergic and application-site adverse events with sofpironium than with vehicle, while the 2025 systematic review reported no serious adverse events in the treated groups. [9][7]
The label reports no significant adverse effects in animal reproduction studies at the doses tested and notes there are no data in pregnant women. [2]

A phase 2 randomized, double-blind trial compared three dosages with vehicle over 42 days in axillary hyperhidrosis. [5] A phase 3 vehicle-controlled trial in Japanese patients treated 5% gel for six weeks, with co-primary endpoints of an HDSS score of 1 or 2 and at least a 50% reduction in gravimetric sweat weight. [1] A 52-week open-label extension followed 185 patients who had completed that trial to assess long-term safety and efficacy. [6] A two-week observational study in routine practice in Japan looked at how early the effect appears. [18]

Two US phase 3 trials, named Cardigan I and II in the publication (registered as BBI-4000-CL-301 and CL-302), enrolled about 350 participants each and tested a 12.45% gel; pooled results were published in 2025. [19][20][10] A separate US safety study ran for longer periods. [21]

The 2025 systematic review covered five studies with 752 patients and reported HDSS responder rates of roughly 54% to 87% in the treated groups, along with greater reductions in sweat weight and DLQI scores than vehicle. [7] A 2026 meta-analysis of five randomized trials (1,398 participants) found a mean sweat-weight reduction of about 25 mg versus vehicle and a risk ratio of 3.27 for achieving a two-point HDSS improvement. [8] Another 2026 meta-analysis of three trials (1,209 patients) reported similar directions for HDSM-Ax, HDSS and DLQI outcomes. [9]
Sofdra is prescription-only in the US, where it was approved in June 2024, and Ecclock is prescription-only in Japan, where it launched in late 2020. [4][2]
